clue.text: East Ender's wife meets important chap in Edam

parts.note: in Cockney speech 'me old Dutch' means my wife (from duchess)
a big cheese is an important person

explanation.surface: A Cockney's wife gets together with a VIP in the Dutch town of Edam.
explanation.walkthrough: Edam looks like the place, but it is the cheese. East Enders are Londoners from the East End, Cockneys, whose slang gives 'Dutch' for wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Edam is a well-known round cheese from the Netherlands, an example of the wider category.

clue.text: Aristocratic lady goes over English version of mashed potatoes

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece going over another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: a duchess is a noblewoman of high rank

explanation.surface: A noblewoman visits England, perhaps crossing the Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes over' places the noblewoman above E in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Duchesse potatoes are mashed potato mixed with egg yolk and piped into rosettes before baking.

clue.text: Gathers plant grown for brewer and school food supplier

parts.note: tucks are folds or gathers sewn into cloth
hops are the climbing plant whose cones flavour beer

explanation.surface: A dressmaker's pleats and a brewer's crop are listed beside a school canteen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tuck' is British school slang for snacks and sweets, sold at the school shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuck shop is a small shop at a British school selling snacks and sweets to pupils.

clue.text: Pitch in with a quiche, a very tasty one

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the run of words quiche, a very

explanation.surface: Someone recommends joining in to share a quiche that tastes very good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch in' reads as a phrase, but 'in' is the signal: the letters run from the end of 'quiche' through 'a' into 'very'.
explanation.definitionFit: To pitch and to heave both mean to throw something heavy with effort.

clue.text: Those have to be cooked on ship for lady receiving guests

indicators.note: food that is cooked is worked over and changed, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: Some dishes must be prepared aboard ship for a woman entertaining visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' fits the kitchen theme, so it reads as cooking rather than as a signal to rearrange 'Those'; 'on' simply joins the ship piece after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who receives and entertains guests at a party or event is its host, in the feminine form.

clue.text: Green peas not as eccentric as table centrepiece

indicators.note: something eccentric is odd or off-centre, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters of these two words form the pool
these letters are removed from the pool, as 'not' says

explanation.surface: Garden peas compared with a showy dish in the middle of the dining table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not as' removes A and S from GREENPEAS, and 'eccentric' rearranges what remains, GREENPE.
explanation.definitionFit: An épergne is an ornamental stand with branching dishes placed in the middle of a dining table.

clue.text: First course includes portion taken from Scotch beefsteak

indicators.note: includes says one piece holds another inside it

parts.note: an entrée is a starter dish served before the main course, in British usage

indicators.note: portion taken from says a few letters are lifted out of the word Scotch

explanation.surface: A starter featuring a slice of Scotch beef.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First course' is the British sense of entrée, a starter; in American usage it means the main course, which would mislead.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrecôte is a boneless steak cut from between the ribs of a beef carcass.

clue.text: Drink up on Saturday

indicators.note: on says one piece follows after the other in this across entry

parts.note: S is a common abbreviation for Saturday

explanation.surface: A command to finish your glass at the weekend.
explanation.definitionFit: To sup is to drink in small mouthfuls, often used of soup or ale.

clue.text: Finds fault with some of chef's cold salads

indicators.note: some of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A diner complains about the cook's chilled salads.
explanation.definitionFit: To scold someone is to tell them off, criticising what they did.

clue.text: Cooking utensil to go in larder

parts.note: a pan is a pot used for cooking
a go is an attempt, so to have a go is to try

explanation.surface: A saucepan is put away in the food cupboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A pantry is a small room or cupboard where food is kept, the same thing as a larder.

clue.text: Military leader repeated: "One drink"

indicators.note: repeated says the leader's letters are written twice

parts.note: CO stands for commanding officer
A means one, as in a single thing

explanation.surface: An officer says it twice before ordering a single drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repeated' gives CO twice, and A follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocoa is a hot drink made from powdered cacao beans and milk.

clue.text: Maize kernels as vegetable or dessert? Hackneyed!

parts.note: a sweet is the British word for a pudding or dessert
corn is trite, sentimental stuff, so corny means hackneyed

explanation.surface: A diner asks whether maize belongs with the main course or the pudding, and finds the question stale.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to 'vegetable'; 'or' is a link, and 'dessert?' sets up the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the variety of maize grown for its sugary kernels, eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: Michaelmas daisy for example in, for example, seasonal chocolate confection

indicators.note: in says the flower and first abbreviation go inside the second one

parts.note: EG again, the abbreviation for for example
the Michaelmas daisy is a kind of aster, a late-flowering plant
EG is the abbreviation of exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: A garden flower is offered as an example of a chocolate treat for the spring holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: The two 'for example' phrases do different jobs: one sits beside the flower, the other wraps round both, so the word splits into E and G.
explanation.definitionFit: This chocolate treat, often hollow, is given at the spring Christian festival.

clue.text: More mature supplier of berries for wine

definitions.meaning: the ... tree bears dark berries used for home-made wine

explanation.definitionFit: Older people are the senior ones; the elder bush supplies elderberries and elderflowers.

clue.text: They are drunk a lot with steamed puddings

definitions.meaning: heavy drinkers who soak up alcohol
light cakes cooked by steaming, a British dessert

explanation.definitionFit: Heavy drinkers soak up drink like a bath item; a steamed sponge is a classic British pudding.

clue.text: Non-vegetarian restaurant where suspects are questioned at length?

definitions.text: where suspects are questioned at length?
definitions.meaning: to grill someone is to interrogate them hard, so a whimsical room for it

explanation.definitionFit: A restaurant serving grilled food bears this name; grilling is slang for intense questioning.

clue.text: Fed orally in school

indicators.note: orally says the word is spoken rather than written

parts.note: something fed to someone has been eaten

explanation.surface: Someone was given food by mouth at a boarding school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orally' looks like part of the feeding picture but signals that a word is spoken. Eton is the famous English public school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College is a famous English boarding school, an example of the category.

clue.text: About to tear into top of eclair that's past its best

parts.note: over can mean about, as in arguing over something
to rip is to tear

indicators.note: top of picks the first letter, which sits at the top of a down entry

explanation.surface: Someone is about to bite into the top of a pastry that has gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' and 'into' are links in a charade; 'top of' gives E from 'eclair'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit that has gone soft and begun to spoil is past its peak condition.

clue.text: Panic over, sailor makes cake with oats and syrup

indicators.note: in a down entry over means placed above, so this piece comes first

parts.note: a flap is a state of panic or agitation
Jack, or Jack tar, is an old name for a sailor

explanation.surface: A seaman, calm again after a scare, bakes an oaty treat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panic over' reads as a phrase, but 'over' puts FLAP above JACK.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the British name for a chewy bar baked from oats, butter and golden syrup.

clue.text: This food comes from France and is hot

parts.note: F is the international vehicle code for France
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A dish is said to originate in France and be served hot.
explanation.definitionFit: Fish is a common food, the flesh of aquatic animals eaten as a meal.

clue.text: Is directed automatically to use side of ham in some recipe

indicators.note: side of picks a letter at the edge, here the first, of the word ham
a recipe is a mix of ingredients, so it signals that letters are mixed up

parts.note: fodder, taken as written
fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook is told to add part of a ham to a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recipe' reads as part of the cooking picture, but it signals a mix of the words 'in some'; 'use' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A missile homes in when guided straight onto its target without human steering.

clue.text: In France a dear and almost totally horrid herb

parts.note: cher is the French word for dear

indicators.note: almost says the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: vile means utterly horrible

explanation.surface: A French endearment is followed by a dreadful-tasting garden plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts VILE to VIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Chervil is a delicate aniseed-flavoured culinary plant, an example of the category.

clue.text: Every year the Fitzgerald girl makes this dish

parts.note: PA stands for per annum, Latin for each year
Ella Fitzgerald was the American jazz singer

explanation.surface: Every year the jazz singer's daughter cooks a Spanish rice dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Ella Fitzgerald was the American jazz singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Paella is a Spanish rice dish with saffron, seafood or chicken, an example of the category.

clue.text: Programme shows sage being topped and chopped up

indicators.note: being topped says the word sage loses its first letter, at the top of a down entry
chopping up breaks something into pieces, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cook shows herbs having their tops cut off before being finely chopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being topped' leaves AGE, and 'chopped up' turns AND into NDA.
explanation.definitionFit: An agenda is a list of items to be dealt with, a programme or plan.

clue.text: Appropriate sort of cake for heavenly creature

definitions.meaning: a light sponge cake named after heavenly beings, fitting here
a celestial being, messenger of God

explanation.definitionFit: Angel cake is a light sponge; a heavenly messenger from God is the second sense.

clue.text: Inferior cheese for use after second portion is returned

indicators.note: after says the word use follows the second, coming later in the entry

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second

indicators.note: is returned says the portion's letters are read backwards

parts.note: a part is a portion

explanation.surface: A bit of poor cheese is kept to bait a trap after a second slice is sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is returned' turns PART into TRAP.
explanation.definitionFit: Mousetrap is a joking British term for cheap, poor-quality cheese, fit only for baiting traps.

clue.text: Bet that's placed in the middle of the mid-morning snack?

indicators.note: placed in the middle of says only the central letters of the snack's name are kept

parts.note: elevenses is the British name for a snack and drink taken around eleven in the morning

explanation.surface: A wager is laid halfway through a morning tea break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'placed in the middle of' keeps the centre of ELEVENSES, dropping EL at the front and ES at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Evens is a betting price where the winnings equal the stake, odds of one to one.

clue.text: Note: tongue's cooked with lobster

parts.note: la is the sixth note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: food that is cooked is altered, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A recipe card says an ox tongue is prepared alongside shellfish.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's of 'tongue's' supplies a real S here, needed in the fodder; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Langouste is the French name for the spiny lobster, a clawless relative of the true lobster.

clue.text: Girl puts wild rice on middle of plate

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so these letters are scrambled
middle of picks the central letter of the five-letter word plate

explanation.surface: A girl serves wild rice in the centre of a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges RICE into ERIC, and 'middle of' gives A from 'plate'. Wild rice is a real grain, so 'wild' hides in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is a girl's given name, an example of the wider category.

clue.text: Turkey's chief means of cooking

definitions.meaning: a commander or chief officer in the Ottoman Empire

explanation.definitionFit: An Ottoman commander bore this title; the Aga stove is a cast-iron British kitchen range.

clue.text: Cook takes a little time first with small cut of meat

indicators.note: first says the little time goes at the front of the entry

parts.note: a minute is a short space of time

indicators.note: to cook is to tamper with, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A chef spends a moment preparing a small piece of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' looks like the chef in the surface, but it is the signal to rearrange 'takes'.
explanation.definitionFit: A minute steak is a thin slice of beef that cooks very quickly.
